1009.title: Gardens with running water
1009.hook: four-part gardens with water channels, reflecting the gardens of the Qur'an
1009.howItsDone: Visitors still walk the channel gardens of places such as the Alhambra's Generalife, Isfahan and the Taj Mahal, and some Muslim homes keep courtyard gardens with a fountain or pool at the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the minaret that lifts the call, and the dome, a sky you can stand under.

"Gardens underneath which rivers flow." That's a phrase from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, describing what waits for those who believe and do good. Now step through a gate into a walled courtyard in Isfahan, or Granada, or Agra. Stone paths cross in the middle. Along each runs a narrow channel of water, so shallow it barely moves, holding a strip of sky. Where the channels meet, there's a pool, or a fountain murmuring. Trees, shade, the smell of wet stone. Today: gardens with running water.
screen: `GARDENS UNDERNEATH WHICH RIVERS FLOW.` → `A WALLED COURTYARD.` → `CHANNELS MEET AT A POOL.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an's word for paradise, jannah, is the ordinary Arabic word for a garden. So when the Qur'an describes the life to come, it describes shade, fruit and water. One passage, in surah forty-seven, even names its rivers: rivers of water that never goes stale, of milk, of wine, of honey. Garden builders worked with a plan often called by a Persian name, chahar bagh, four gardens: a walled rectangle split by water channels into four parts that meet at a center. Some readers link those channels to the rivers of surah forty-seven. Others point out that walled Persian gardens are older than Islam, and say Muslims took up the old plan and gave it new meaning. Both can be true. Either way, think what water meant to the builders. Isfahan, Agra and Granada are hot in summer. Water you could hear was wealth. Water you could see moving was life. A garden with running water was a small earthly reminder of a promise, built by hand, to be walked in. And these gardens were made for sitting, not racing through: sitting beside a channel in the shade, and listening. Some were planted around tombs, so the dead rested inside a picture of the garden they hoped for. In the Qur'an the garden is a promise. The garden on earth kept that promise in view. Under which rivers flow.

segments.voice: Sit near water or a plant, a glass on the table, a tap running into a bowl, a houseplant, a tree outside, and look at it as the center of a garden, where all the paths meet. Listen to the water or watch the light on it; with a plant, choose one leaf and take in its edge, its color, the way it turns toward the light. If you pray, you can say al-hamdu lillah, praise be to God, for water; if you don't, just stay with it.
Jannah. The Qur'an's word for paradise and garden, pictured as gardens under which rivers flow, and echoed in walled courtyards split by channels. Today's word.
Your line: under which rivers flow. Shade, water, and a place to sit. Until tomorrow.

1010.title: Carpets and tiles
1010.hook: prayer rugs, Persian carpets, Iznik tiles
1010.howItsDone: At home or at work, a Muslim may pray on a prayer rug laid toward Mecca, though any clean place is enough; mosque floors are commonly carpeted, and some Ottoman mosques are lined with Iznik tiles.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jannah, the garden, and the walled courtyard gardens under which rivers flow.

At prayer time, in the corner of an office, someone unrolls a small rectangle of cloth, smooths a wrinkle with one hand, checks the direction, and steps onto it. A minute ago this was the spot by the printer. Now it's a place of prayer. Far away, in an old mosque in Istanbul, the walls are covered in tiles: deep blue, turquoise, and a red like a ripe tomato, painted with tulips and carnations. Underfoot, a carpet. On the walls, a garden in glazed clay. Cloth and clay. Today: mihrab.
screen: `A RUG UNROLLED BY THE PRINTER.` → `A MOSQUE WALL OF TILES.` → `CLOTH AND CLAY.`

segments.voice: Start with the rug. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says the earth has been made for him a place of prayer, and pure. Any clean ground will do. So a prayer rug isn't required. It does a quieter job: it marks off a clean patch of floor, and lets someone carry a place of prayer rolled up under one arm. Another hadith in al-Bukhari mentions the Prophet praying on a small mat. On many prayer rugs the weaver puts an arch at one end, the shape of the mihrab, the niche in a mosque wall that shows the direction of prayer. Lay the rug the right way, and the little arch points where to face. Then there are the great carpets, Persian, Turkish and more, knotted by hand. Some are woven as gardens, yesterday's channels and all. The Qur'an's own picture of paradise has carpets in it. In Pickthall's translation: "And silken carpets spread." Now the tiles. In the town of Iznik, in Turkey, potters made tiles in white, cobalt blue and turquoise, with a red that sits up slightly from the glaze. The Ottomans lined mosques with them, so tulips climb the walls around the people praying. One more thing, because it gets told a lot: people say weavers leave a deliberate mistake in every carpet, because only God is perfect. It's a story people tell. There's no sure source behind it, and a weaver's mistakes can arrive on their own. Woven prayer.

Someone put every crossing there, by hand or with a machine someone built and tended; think of those hands for a moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them; if you don't, just thank them quietly, wherever they are.

1011.title: The Burdah
1011.hook: al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet ﷺ, sung across the world
1011.howItsDone: In Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa and South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing the Burdah, often around the Prophet's birthday; other Muslims, following reformist scholars, do not recite it or object to some of its lines.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mihrab, carpets and tiles: a rug with a little arch, tulips on a mosque wall, woven prayer.

A poet lies in bed in Egypt, half his body unable to move. That's how the story people tell about Sharaf al-Din al-Busiri begins. With nothing left to him but words, he composes a long poem praising the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and recites it, weeping, over and over. One night he dreams the Prophet stands beside him, passes his hand over him, and lays his cloak, his burdah, across his body. In the morning, the story says, al-Busiri gets up and walks out of the house. Today: the Burdah.
screen: `A POET WHO CANNOT MOVE.` → `A DREAM, AND A CLOAK.` → `IN THE MORNING, HE WALKS.`

segments.voice: Whether someone hears that healing as a miracle, a blessing or a story, the poem itself is real, and it traveled. People simply call it the Burdah, the poem of the cloak. It opens the old way Arabic poems opened, with longing: a lover remembering a place and a neighbor, unable to stop his tears. Then it turns. The poet confesses his own faults and warns his soul against its appetites. Then he pours out praise: the Prophet's birth, his night journey, his patience, his mercy. Every line ends on the same rhyme, the letter mim, so the whole poem rings like one long bell. And people sang it. Across Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa, South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing it together, often with a refrain between verses, often around the Prophet's birthday. Why praise the Prophet in poetry at all? Those who love the Burdah point to a verse of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." A poem like this is one way of answering that. Not every Muslim sings it. Some scholars, especially in reform movements, have objected to a few of its lines, saying they ask of the Prophet what only God can give. Those who love the poem read the same lines as asking for his intercession, which they believe God grants. Both sides would say they are guarding the Prophet's honor. And the poem keeps being sung. The poem of the cloak.

segments.voice: Play the opening of a recording of the Burdah if you can, or hum a soft mmm on each out-breath, like its one rhyme, and listen to how the voices repeat and the refrain comes back around. If you pray, you can send blessings on the Prophet with the words Muslims use, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam; if you don't, simply listen to people praising someone they love.
The Burdah. Al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet, every line rhymed on one letter, sung in many lands. Today's word.
Your line: the poem of the cloak. Longing, then confession, then praise, all on one rhyme. See you tomorrow.

1012.title: The voice
1012.hook: the adhan and Qur'an recited in maqams, melodic modes
1012.howItsDone: Muslims learn tajwid from teachers, often in mosque classes, and listen to celebrated reciters; muezzins in different cities call the same words of the adhan in their own local melodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Burdah, al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, rhymed on a single letter.

Two recordings of the same call to prayer. In the first, the muezzin's voice rises slowly, leans on one note, falls, and rises again, with something like an ache in it. In the second, the voice is brighter and quicker, climbing in little steps. The words are the same in both, line for line. The tune is not. Neither melody is written down as sheet music. They live in the throat, passed from teacher to student. Today, the last stop among the arts: the voice.
screen: `TWO RECORDINGS, ONE CALL.` → `SAME WORDS, DIFFERENT TUNES.` → `IT LIVES IN THE THROAT.`

segments.voice: Calligraphy, geometry, the vine, the dome, the garden, the carpet, the poem: the arts end where a Muslim day begins, with a voice. The Qur'an asks to be recited. In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measure." And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, tells people to beautify the Qur'an with their voices. So there are rules, called tajwid: how long to hold a vowel, which letters press against each other, where to stop and where never to stop. Tajwid governs the sounds. It doesn't fix the melody. Into that space come the maqamat, the melodic modes of Arab music, with names like bayati, hijaz, rast and saba. Each has its own color; some listeners hear saba as sorrowful and hijaz as reaching. A skilled reciter may move from one mode to another as the verses shift, from warning to mercy, from story to promise. Here Muslims differ, and fairly. Some scholars warn against reciting by musical rules, afraid the tune will start to bend the words. Others welcome the modes, as long as tajwid comes first. Both would say the words lead and the voice serves. The call to prayer works the same way: fixed words, and melodies that change from Cairo to Istanbul to Jakarta. No instrument. No score. Only a human voice, trained and offered to God. The voice is the art.

segments.voice: Play a minute each of two adhans from different places, or, if you can't right now, listen to the room around you and to your own breath. Don't follow the words; follow the shape: where the voice rises, where it holds, where it falls. If you pray, you can answer the call quietly, repeating its words after the muezzin; if you don't, just listen.
The voice. The Qur'an and the call to prayer, sung with no instrument, shaped by the rules of tajwid and colored by melodic modes. Today's word.

1013.title: The endowment
1013.hook: a property given forever for good: a well, a school, a hospital
1013.howItsDone: Muslims still found waqfs for mosques, schools, wells and scholarships, often through charities that manage the endowment and spend only its income, and speak of it as sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the voice. Tajwid sets the sounds, the melody serves the words, and that closed the arts.

Umar ibn al-Khattab had come into a piece of land at Khaybar, and, as he put it, he had never owned anything he valued more. He went to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asked what to do with it. The answer, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, comes to this: if you wish, keep the land itself, and give away what it produces. So Umar did. The land could not be sold, given or inherited. Its harvest went to the poor, to relatives, to freeing slaves, to the cause of God, to travelers and to guests. Keep the root. Give the fruit. A new part of the path begins: institutions. Today: the endowment.
screen: `UMAR'S LAND AT KHAYBAR.` → `KEEP THE ROOT, GIVE THE FRUIT.` → `A NEW PART: INSTITUTIONS.`

segments.voice: The word is waqf: property set aside so it can never be sold, with its income given for good, on and on. You've met waqf at work on this path already: the hospitals that sent no bill, the colleges where students got a room and bread. Here's the idea underneath. A gift usually ends. You give a meal, and it's eaten. A waqf is built not to end. A row of shops is endowed, and their rent pays a teacher. A farm is endowed, and its grain feeds the hungry. The giver dies. The shops are still rented. The teacher is still paid. Why give this way? A saying of the Prophet in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that brings benefit, and a righteous child who prays for them. Ongoing charity, sadaqah jariyah, charity that keeps flowing. A waqf is that hadith set in stone and soil. And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love." Umar gave the land he valued most. Sultans endowed mosques and hospitals. Ordinary people, women and men, endowed a fountain, a shelf of books, a bed in a hospital. Some waqfs fed people long after their founders died. Others were mismanaged, seized, or simply forgotten; forever is a hard promise for human hands to keep. Today some Muslims are reviving the idea, with endowed wells, scholarships and funds. Given forever.

1014.title: The school
1014.hook: the madrasah teaching Qur'an, law, language and more
1014.howItsDone: Muslim children and adults study in mosque circles and madrasahs of every kind, from weekend Qur'an classes to seminaries; in traditional study a student may still receive an ijazah from a teacher, naming the chain of teachers behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: waqf, the endowment. Keep the root, give the fruit: given forever.

A pillar in a big mosque. A teacher sits with his back against it, a book open on his knees. Around him on the floor, in a half circle, his students: a boy from the town, an old merchant, a traveler who arrived last week. He reads a line, explains it, and they write. When the lesson ends, they stand up and the circle disappears. Tomorrow it forms again at the same pillar. That circle is called a halaqa, and learning in Muslim lands often happened in circles like it, before there was any building called a school. Today: the school.
screen: `A TEACHER AGAINST A PILLAR.` → `A HALF CIRCLE ON THE FLOOR.` → `THE HALAQA.`

segments.voice: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim, makes a promise: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, God makes easy for them a road to paradise. So people traveled, and sat in circles. Over time the circles needed rooms, food, books and paid teachers, and the madrasah grew around them. You met the great colleges of Baghdad and Fez earlier on this path. Today, step inside an ordinary one. A courtyard with a fountain. Small rooms around it where students lived. A prayer hall. A shelf of books. Classes in Qur'an and hadith, law and Arabic grammar, and in some, logic or arithmetic. And at the end, no diploma from the building. Instead, a person. You met the calligrapher's license a few days ago; the schools had their own. A teacher could give you an ijazah, written permission to teach a book, naming who had taught it to him, and who had taught that teacher, back through a chain of names. The knowledge belonged to the chain, not to the walls. One more surprise: in Arabic, madrasah simply means school. Any school. A child in Cairo goes to a madrasah to learn math and science. Places to learn.

What did they hand you that you still carry? If you pray, you can pray for them, living or gone; if you don't, just hold their face in mind for a moment.
The school. From the halaqa at a mosque pillar to the madrasah with its courtyard, its students and its chain of teachers. Today's word.

1015.title: The road houses
1015.hook: caravanserais on trade routes, where travelers stayed
1015.howItsDone: Muslim travelers shorten their prayers on journeys and may postpone a Ramadan fast; zakat and other charity can go to the wayfarer, and restored caravanserais and khans still stand in cities and along old routes in Turkey, Iran and the Arab world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the school. A circle at a pillar, a courtyard of students, a chain of teachers: places to learn.

A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is startlingly honest: travel is a piece of torment. It keeps you from your sleep, your food and your drink, so when you've finished what you went for, hurry home to your family. Anyone who has slept on an airport floor knows. The old trade roads were harder: dust by day, cold at night, thieves in the hills. Along them, people built houses for exactly that torment. You met the Seljuk ones in Anatolia; this time, the idea underneath them all. Today: the road houses.
screen: `TRAVEL IS A PIECE OF TORMENT.` → `HURRY HOME.` → `HOUSES ALONG THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with how the faith treats the traveler, because the stone follows from it. The Qur'an makes room for someone on the road. A person on a journey in Ramadan may leave the fast and make up the days later, it says in surah two. And prayer may be shortened. In Pickthall's translation: "And when ye go forth in the land, it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship." The verse goes on to name the fear of attack. In Sahih Muslim, someone later asks Umar why people still shorten, now that the roads are safe. Umar says he wondered the same and asked the Prophet, who called it a charity from God, to be accepted. The Qur'an also names ibn al-sabil, the son of the road, the wayfarer, among those owed a share of charity. So the law leans toward the tired, and the road house leans the same way. Out on the open road it was called a caravanserai; inside a city, often a khan. Most share a pattern: one great gate shut at night, a courtyard open to the sky, a well or fountain, rooms around the edge for people, stalls or arcades for the animals, often a small mosque. In cities the khan was also a warehouse and market, where far-off merchants stored bales and struck deals. On the road it was shelter, and in some, paid for by waqf, the night cost nothing. A road house turns a stranger into a guest for a night. But the honest hadith still holds: a road house isn't home. It's a place to gather strength to keep going, or to go back. Rest for the traveler.
screen: `THE LAW MAKES ROOM FOR THE ROAD.` · `IBN AL-SABIL, SON OF THE ROAD.` · `CARAVANSERAI AND KHAN.` · `A GUEST FOR A NIGHT.` · then, large: `REST FOR THE TRAVELER.`
